title: Show HN: Pizza – An event-driven AI agent, no while true
summary: Hi HN, I made Pizza, an open-source, event-driven AI agent. No `while true`. Each turn is a state machine. Conversations and tool calls go into an immutable SQLite log. The UI, model context, and session tree are built from that log. The model gets one tool: a CLI. Reading files, editing code, and running commands all go through it. You can keep a conversation going without manually starting new sessions. Pizza compacts context as needed, and you can branch from any earlier message. Agents in separate workspaces talk through `tell`, each doing the work in its own project. An SSH host can be a workspace too: Pizza deploys itself there and runs remotely. Desktop and terminal interfaces are included. Bring your own model. https://github.com/pizza-agent/pizza
story_key: story|title:pizza an event driven ai agent no while true
content_excerpt: Your desktop companion for code, ideas, and everyday work. Keeps the conversation going, with your apps connected. Events keep the work connected. Explore the choices behind Pizza’s memory, tools, and interfaces. Reactor advances each turn through an event-driven state machine. The immutable SQLite event log is the source for the interface, model context, and history tree. Interrupts, retries, and parallel tool calls have explicit handlers. Recorded events make state easier to rebuild and inspect. Fork from a message in the past. Continue along a new branch while keeping the earlier path available to revisit and compare. A continuing conversation and a branchable history work together. Context compaction helps the conversation keep going. The model calls a single CLI tool. Reading, writing, editing, and workspace messaging are commands behind that interface. A small tool schema reduces repeated definitions in the model context. Extra instructions and capabilities can be loaded as needed. The desktop GUI, terminal UI, JSON-RPC, and one-shot print mode consume the same SessionFacade event stream. Use Pizza interactively, automate a task, or embed it in your own tooling. The interfaces share the same agent runtime. Go from a rough idea to something real. Pizza works in your projects, keeps the context, and helps you carry the work forward. Give your personal assistant a goal. Project agents work in their own context and send the results back. You do not need to start a fresh session for every task. Pizza manages the context as the work continues. Old tool results are masked and context is compacted when needed, reducing what the model carries into the next turn. Keep your projects, conversations, and recurring work connected to the same agent. Connect over SSH. Pizza deploys the agent to the remote host, where it works with that project’s files and tools. Slack, Discord, Telegram, Lark, voice, and webhooks can all reach the same agent through the gateway. Schedule checks, summaries, and routine tasks. The persistent assistant can pick them up on a recurring schedule. Channels, voice, and remote access require their corresponding service and account setup. Bring your files, conversations, and projects into the work. Connect an app, sign in, and let Pizza help with the next step. Connections depend on your Pizza version, account permissions, and provider setup. Open source means you can see how Pizza works, make it your own, and help shape what comes next. Pizz

title: FlashVMM – jail your AI agent in a MicroVM that boots in 18 ms
story_key: story|title:flashvmm jail your ai agent in a microvm that boots in 18 ms
content_excerpt: A sandbox for AI runs: every agent task gets its own FlashVM. It's claimed warm in milliseconds, runs whatever the agent wrote behind a real hypervisor boundary, and is thrown away when the task ends. One install, no account, no cloud. We built our own virtual machine for this: FlashVM , leaner and faster than a conventional microVM. PowerShell as Administrator. It enables the hypervisor if needed, picks x64 or ARM64 and verifies the checksum. Then jail the agent you already use, unchanged: flash agents setup , then cd my-project && claude . It runs in its own VM and sees only that folder. The full tour: flash demo . Scripts, package installs, test suites, and Docker builds run inside a VM with its own kernel. Cap CPU, memory, disk and network only when you want to, and decide what it may reach with --egress . Nothing touches the host. flash-mcp hands Claude, Cursor or any MCP client the whole lifecycle in 21 tools: create, run commands, copy files, fork, limit what it can reach, call APIs without holding the key, watch, snapshot, restore, tear down. Warm pools keep spares already running, so a task claims one instead of booting. Snapshots restore a prepared environment in milliseconds, and flash fork branches a running VM into copies that carry on from where it was. A GPU pool loads an AI model on the host's GPU once and every VM you allow sends it requests. No VM touches the GPU or needs a driver, and snapshots and warm pools keep working. Metal on Apple silicon, Vulkan on Linux and Windows. The task takes a warm spare from the pool, or restores a snapshot. No kernel boot on the hot path. The agent's commands run in the guest with flash exec ; exit code, stdout and stderr come back structured. Files go in and out with flash cp ; logs, metrics and events stream back live. The VM is removed when the task ends. Nothing it did carries into the next run, unless you snapshot it.

title: Show HN: db-branch – database branches in seconds for AI agents and CI, via ZFS
story_key: story|title:db branch database branches in seconds for ai agents and ci via zfs
content_excerpt: Instant MySQL database branches on ZFS clones, clustered across VMs with ProxySQL routing Test a migration, let an AI agent loose, or give every pull request its own copy of the database. db-branch creates a copy-on-write branch of a large database in seconds, with nothing copied. Break it, reset it, throw it away. Built on ZFS clones, self-hosted, Apache-2.0. Status: Beta. db-branch is usable today, but APIs and command-line details may still change before 1.0. It is an independent open-source project, built from scratch. In your browser, 0 minutes. A live console demo runs entirely in the page (nothing real is created): https://demo.db-branch.com/ On a Mac or Windows machine, about 2 minutes. db-branch needs Linux and ZFS, so run it in an Ubuntu VM with Multipass . One command makes the VM, installs db-branch, initialises it on a file-backed ZFS pool and loads a small sample base, shop (MySQL 8.4): On Windows (PowerShell or cmd), put the multipass launch command on one line and drop the \ : Requirements: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or 26.04 LTS, and a ZFS pool (the zfsutils-linux package is installed as a dependency). The repository signing key fingerprint is 3F404C4E5D49FA653F8385692C6E89E341D4D7A5 . db-branch init prints the initial admin password once. MySQL works the same way, for example mysql@8.4.13 . List installable versions with db-branch runtime available . To try a version upgrade on one MySQL branch: A base is a ZFS dataset holding a loaded database. A branch is a ZFS clone of a base snapshot, so creating one copies nothing, and each branch runs its own database server on its own port. Optionally, ProxySQL routes client connections to the right branch by user name (or by a /*db_branch='name'*/ query comment). Several nodes form a Raft cluster that shares bases, branches, settings and users. db-branch は、ZFS クローンで MySQL / PostgreSQL のデータベースブランチを発行・リセット・破棄するツールです。現在は Beta で、1.0 までに API が変わる可能性があります。コアは Apache-2.0 で、有償モジュール（認証/SSO・監査・履歴・差分・FSx ストレージ）は別パッケージ（クローズドソース、セルフホスト、ライセンスキー）です。 Mac / Windows では、Multipass のコマンド1つで試せます: https://db-branch.com/ja/docs/getting-started/#multipass-ですぐ試す 。日本語のサイトは https://db-branch.com/ja/ 、設計ドキュメントは docs/ にあります（日本語）。 Instant MySQL database branches on ZFS clones, clustered across VMs with ProxySQL routing

title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
summary: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
summary: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
summary: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.
